title: Too Tough, Says the Man Who Just Promoted Tough: The Week, Unwrapped
dek: Trump hands the White House to his immigration architect, then calls the policy too tough. Plus Musk's half-billion-dollar flop, Nvidia's board asks questions, and Schumer brings razor wire.
body:
## Friday: promote the plan. Sunday: blame the plan.

Welcome to the week after the midterms, where everyone in Washington is processing their feelings, and some of them are processing them on camera.

Let's start at the White House. Three days after Republicans lost Congress, President Trump announced on Truth Social that Stephen Miller would replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff [1]. Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors" and said Wiles "has done a great job!" and would move to his political operation [2]. Miller, currently deputy chief of staff, joined Trump's 2016 campaign as a speechwriter and is a key architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies [1]. Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming Oversight chair, called him "the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids" [2].

So that was Friday. On Sunday, CBS published Trump's 60 Minutes interview, taped three days after the election, in which he said of his deportation policy, "So I think it was too tough" [3]. He added that he gets "hurt because we also took people that had good jobs" [3].

Let's line those up. Friday: "The immigration guy is now running the building." Sunday: "The immigration thing may have been a bit much." That's not a course correction. That's a man saying the soup was too salty while handing the salt shaker a promotion. CBS notes Miller pushed ICE to aim for 3,000 arrests a day last year [3]. Somewhere, a pollster is staring at that sentence like it's a magic-eye poster.

## Elon Musk, venture capitalist of defeat

Speaking of returns on investment: Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million to elect Republicans this cycle, according to FEC filings reported by Forbes, more than three times the next-largest donors [4]. He backed Republicans in 106 House and Senate races; as of Wednesday, 18 had won, mostly in safe red areas, 45 had lost and 43 were uncalled [4]. About $225 million went to Texas alone, where Democrats flipped both a Senate seat and the governorship [4].

Half a billion dollars. For 18 wins, mostly in places that were going to vote Republican if the candidate was a folding chair. That's roughly the business model of buying a lottery ticket after the numbers are announced, and still losing. Investor Steve Rattner went further, posting that 98 percent of Musk's candidate-specific money went to losers [4]. That's Rattner's math, not ours, but if it's even close, Musk has finally found a rocket that only goes down.

## Nvidia's board has a few questions

Over at Nvidia, the board announced an independent investigation on Sunday after reporting that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort [5]. A committee of independent directors, with outside counsel, will run it, and the board says it has no reason to think national security or company secrets were compromised [5].

The reporting, per PC Gamer's roundup: Axios obtained a draft apology to employees in which Huang admits an affair, and the New York Times reported the Trump administration suspects the woman, an executive at the Singapore cloud firm Megaspeed, of passing information to China's Ministry of State Security [6]. That is an allegation, not a finding, and China denies it [6]. Nvidia had earlier disputed reports of a romantic relationship and called it professional [6]. Huang's draft reportedly says he is "fully committed to Nvidia" and isn't stepping down [6].

We are not here to grade anybody's marriage. We are here to point out that the company at the center of America's AI-chip export fight [6] had disputed the romance reporting, and then its board launched an investigation into the thing there was nothing to see about [5][6]. Corporate governance: it's like regular governance, but the voters are hedge funds.

## And the winners, briefly gracious

Democrats, meanwhile, won the Senate too, and will hold at least 54 seats in January, by CBS's count, with Alaska and Mississippi still counting [7]. Chuck Schumer celebrated with, "Against all odds, we Democrats have won the Senate" [7], and vowed to tie Trump up in "legislative razor wire" if he defies the law [7].

Razor wire. A bold metaphor from the party that spent the last two years mostly armed with strongly worded letters. Democrats now have both chambers [2][7] and, for the first time in a while, no one else to blame. Which means the razor wire is either a real plan or the most aggressive thing ever said by a man who has definitely owned a fleece vest.

So: one side promoted the plan it now says was too tough, a billionaire bought half a billion dollars of nothing, a chip giant's board is investigating what it said wasn't there, and the winners are promising barbed wire. Two years until the next one. Pace yourselves.
